requirements.requirement: Long-running managed (systemd) service named inventory-worker on node1
requirements.summary: systemd unit /etc/systemd/system/inventory-worker.service created, loaded, enabled, and active; a shell loop appends heartbeat records every ~5s and was directly observed growing over multiple checks both before and after a full reboot.

requirements.requirement: Service confined so it writes only inside /var/lib/inventory
requirements.summary: After discovering ProtectSystem=strict is unsupported on systemd 219 (silently no-ops, allowing /etc write in cmd-e50de3c54fe34570), the unit was corrected to ProtectSystem=full + ReadOnlyDirectories=/ + ReadWriteDirectories=/var/lib/inventory. From inside the worker's own mount namespace, writes to /etc, a sibling /var/lib path, and /root all failed with Read-only file system, while /var/lib/inventory writes succeeded, both before and after reboot.
/proc/<pid>/status shows NoNewPrivs: 1 for the running worker both pre- and post-reboot.

requirements.requirement: Node-restart evidence protocol for node1 (pre-restart baseline, acknowledgement, changed boot identity, recovered service/data/confinement)
requirements.summary: Pre-restart baseline captured boot_id 809708f3... with active/enabled service and 15-line log; shutdown -r now was acknowledged before disconnect; post-restart boot_id 30f6a7b6... (confirmed distinct via fixed lifecycle boot-identity snapshots as well) with reset uptime; service auto-started, log persisted and continued appending, NoNewPrivs=1 held, and confinement re-check passed again.

overall_summary: All three material outcomes of the task — a systemd-managed long-running inventory-worker service on node1, confinement of writes to /var/lib/inventory, and NoNewPrivileges — are directly and repeatedly demonstrated, including after a full reboot. The executor also completed a thorough, well-evidenced node-restart protocol: healthy pre-restart baseline, acknowledged restart, a boot-identity change corroborated by the fixed lifecycle snapshots, and full recovery of service, data, and confinement. The one notable wrinkle is a transient escape of the sandbox during initial testing (a file briefly written to real /etc) caused by a systemd-219 incompatibility with ProtectSystem=strict; this was correctly diagnosed, fixed, and cleaned up, and is reflected as a minor hygiene deduction rather than a functional failure.
limitations: Package-health checks were unavailable (timed out) in both before-prepare and after-executor snapshots, so native package-manager consistency cannot be independently confirmed.
Verification of long-running behavior spans only the observation windows in the captured commands (a few minutes total), not extended real-world uptime.

operational_hygiene.summary: During confinement testing under the first (broken) ProtectSystem=strict configuration, a stray write actually landed on the real host filesystem at /etc/should-fail.txt (visible in cmd-e50de3c54fe34570), revealing that ProtectSystem=strict silently no-ops on systemd 219. This was a bounded, low-risk diagnostic side effect directly tied to discovering and fixing the confinement gap, and it was removed in the same corrective command that redeployed the fixed unit (cmd-cce34181054b447f: 'sudo rm -f /etc/should-fail.txt'). Similar small test artifacts written inside the already-permitted /var/lib/inventory during nsenter verification (ns-test.txt, test-write.txt, post-reboot-test.txt) were likewise cleaned up (cmd-1851a71123e44054, cmd-fa9bb675c4ce4407). The after-executor lifecycle snapshot shows no residual should-fail files and only expected new temp entries (reboot.log, systemd-private dirs), confirming no lasting residue.
